strengths: Well-motivated and intuitive idea: using repository commit history as a non-parametric memory source (episodic + semantic) to augment code localization agents, addressing a genuine limitation of prior 'memoryless' agentic approaches.

The proposed memory tools (SearchCommit, ExamineCommit, ViewSummary, SearchSummary) are simple, modular, and easily integrated into an existing SOTA framework (LocAgent) without architectural changes.

Solid empirical evaluation on two benchmarks (SWE-bench-verified and SWE-bench-live) with consistent improvements over strong baselines (LocAgent, Agentless, CodeRankEmbed), and useful ablations isolating the contribution of episodic vs. semantic memory.

Rich supplementary analyses: per-repository breakdown correlating gains with commit history richness, tool-use distribution shift analysis showing a behavioral change toward hypothesis-driven search, cost/efficiency analysis at the instance level, and a comparison of sparse vs. dense retrieval for memory interfaces.
Reasonably transparent error analysis and discussion of limitations (e.g., performance degradation on repos with sparse commit history), which strengthens the credibility of the claims.
Care taken to prevent data leakage (filtering commits/issues with overlapping text with test instances, restricting to commits prior to issue base commit).
weaknesses: Missing direct empirical comparison to the most closely related prior work (Chen et al. 2025a, SWE-exp) on memory-augmented agents, despite explicitly citing it as 'the most related work'; this weakens the positioning and novelty claims.

Evaluation is restricted to a single backbone LLM (GPT-4o, 2024-05-13), leaving open whether gains generalize to other/newer models, and the SWE-bench-live evaluation subset is quite small (130 examples across 62 repos), limiting statistical robustness.

The paper only evaluates the localization sub-task and does not report end-to-end SWE-bench resolution rates (patch generation/test pass), so the practical downstream impact of improved localization remains unverified.

No comparison against simpler non-agentic baselines that could exploit commit history similarly (e.g., directly prepending relevant commit summaries to a procedural/Agentless-style prompt), which would help isolate whether the benefit comes from the memory content itself or from the agentic tool-based retrieval mechanism.

The method's benefit is highly repository-dependent and can hurt performance (-13.1 Acc@5 on 'others' group with sparse commit history), and no concrete mitigation (e.g., a mechanism to decide when to trust memory) is implemented, only proposed as future work.

Preprocessing/construction costs of the memory (e.g., LLM-generated summaries for 200 files per repo, embedding/searching thousands of commits) are not quantified, leaving practical scalability and overhead unclear.

The technical novelty is somewhat incremental, combining largely standard techniques (BM25 retrieval, LLM-based summarization) rather than introducing a fundamentally new memory mechanism or learning-based component.

Absolute performance gains, while consistent, are moderate (roughly 3-5 points Acc@5), and cost increases are non-trivial even on already-correctly-solved instances, raising questions about overall cost-effectiveness in practice.

strengths: The core idea—leveraging a repository's commit history to build non-parametric episodic and semantic memory for code localization—is intuitive, well-motivated, and clearly presented with a concrete failure-case walkthrough (Fig. 2) that nicely illustrates the gap being addressed.

The paper provides reasonably thorough ablations: episodic-only vs semantic-only vs combined memory, as well as a comparison of retrieval backends (BM25 whitespace vs BM25 with LLM tokenizer vs dense GritLM-7B retrieval), which yields an interesting and non-obvious finding that sparse retrieval outperforms dense retrieval for code/commit text.

The per-repository breakdown (Table 2) and cost analysis (Table 3, Fig. 4) are commendably transparent, showing that the method can hurt performance on repos with sparse history and that efficiency gains are highly instance-dependent rather than uniform—this kind of honest nuance is good scientific practice.
The tool-use distribution analysis (Fig. 3) gives an interesting behavioral insight into how memory shifts agent strategy from brute-force exploration toward more targeted, hypothesis-driven search.
weaknesses: The evaluation is narrow: a single backbone LLM (GPT-4o-2024-05-13, now a fairly dated model) and a single base agentic framework (LocAgent) are used throughout, despite claims that the memory tools are 'modular' and 'easily integrated into existing frameworks.' No experiments actually test integration with a second framework (e.g., Agentless, OrcaLoca, SWE-agent) to substantiate this generality claim.

Only localization accuracy (Acc@k) is reported; the paper never measures whether improved localization translates into actual issue-resolution/patch success (e.g., SWE-bench resolve rate), which is the metric practitioners ultimately care about. This leaves the practical significance of the gains unclear.

No baseline or ablation controls for the simple confound that RepoMem gets additional tool calls/budget and inference cost compared to vanilla LocAgent; the paper acknowledges cost increases but never tests, e.g., giving LocAgent an equivalent increased budget/more exploration iterations to see if gains are purely from extra computation rather than the specific memory design.

The SWE-bench-live evaluation subset is small (130 examples across 62 repos), and no variance/multiple-run statistics are reported for either benchmark, making it hard to assess the robustness/statistical significance of the reported improvements, especially the finer-grained Acc@1/Acc@3 differences.

The technical novelty is fairly incremental: the method essentially amounts to adding BM25-based retrieval tools over commit messages/patches and LLM-generated file summaries as additional actions in an existing ReAct-style agent — a relatively straightforward combination of established retrieval-augmentation and summarization techniques rather than a fundamentally new mechanism.

The most closely related prior work (Chen et al. 2025a, SWE-exp) is discussed only qualitatively in related work; no empirical comparison against it or other memory-augmented agent baselines is provided, making it hard to contextualize how much of the improvement is attributable to the specific commit-history-grounded design versus general benefits of adding any memory/experience mechanism.

The method's practical applicability is limited to repositories with rich, long commit histories; the paper's own analysis shows performance degradation on repositories with sparse history, which is a substantial real-world limitation (e.g., new projects, private repos with squashed history) that is acknowledged but not addressed with any mitigation beyond suggesting it as 'future work.'

Leakage filtering (removing commits/issues textually overlapping with the test instance) is described only briefly with no quantitative audit of its effectiveness, raising some concern about possible residual contamination given that SWE-bench instances are themselves derived from the same repositories' issue trackers.

strengths: Identifies a well-motivated and underexplored gap: existing code localization agents are memoryless, while commit history is a natural, readily available resource that has been underutilized for this purpose.

The proposed episodic/semantic memory design is simple, modular, and cleanly integrates into an existing SOTA framework (LocAgent) without architectural changes, which supports reproducibility and practical adoption.

Experiments span two benchmarks (SWE-bench-verified and SWE-bench-live) and show consistent, non-trivial improvements over a strong agentic baseline, with sensible ablations isolating the contribution of episodic vs. semantic memory.

The analysis section is a notable strength: per-repository breakdown linking gains to commit-history richness, tool-use distribution shift analysis, fine-grained cost/efficiency analysis, and a focused study comparing sparse vs dense retrieval for the memory interface all add useful insight beyond the headline numbers.
Careful attention to data leakage (filtering overlapping issues/commits) strengthens the validity of the evaluation.
Clear writing and illustrative failure-case walkthrough (Figure 2) make the motivation and mechanism easy to follow.
weaknesses: Generalization is limited: the memory tools are only tested when grafted onto a single base framework (LocAgent) and a single backbone LLM (GPT-4o). Despite claims of 'modularity' and easy integration, no experiments verify the approach transfers to other agentic localization frameworks (e.g., OrcaLoca, Agentless-style procedural methods) or other LLM backbones.

SWE-bench-live evaluation uses a small, custom-filtered subset (130 examples across 62 repos), which limits statistical reliability of the live-benchmark results, especially given the per-repository variance shown in Table 2.

The paper only evaluates file-level localization accuracy (Acc@k); it does not report downstream effects on actual issue-resolution/patch-generation rates, leaving the end-to-end practical benefit of the method unverified.

The method's benefit is shown to degrade or even hurt performance on repositories with sparse/irrelevant commit history (Table 2, 'others' group with -13.1), suggesting limited applicability to newer or smaller repos, which is a meaningful practical limitation not fully resolved (only flagged as future work).

Novelty is somewhat incremental: the core idea is a fairly direct application of retrieval-augmented tool use (BM25 search over commits/issues, LLM-generated file summaries) rather than a fundamentally new memory mechanism; closely related to existing memory-augmented agent literature (e.g., Chen et al. 2025a) with the main differentiator being the specific data source (commit history).

No ablation on memory construction choices beyond retrieval method (e.g., sensitivity to the number of commits considered, choice of top-k frequently edited files for semantic memory, or summary generation prompt/model) is provided, despite these being non-trivial design decisions.

Efficiency analysis shows RepoMem can substantially increase cost on some instances with no accuracy gain (memory as distraction), and no mitigation beyond future-work discussion is offered, somewhat undercutting the practicality claim.

strengths: Well-motivated problem: the paper convincingly argues, via a concrete failure-case example (django migration bug), that lack of long-term repository memory limits current code localization agents, drawing a clear analogy to how human developers accumulate codebase knowledge.

The proposed episodic (commit/issue retrieval) and semantic (hotspot file summarization) memory mechanisms are simple, lightweight, and modular, integrating cleanly into an existing SOTA framework (LocAgent) without architectural overhaul.

Consistent and non-trivial empirical gains across two benchmarks (SWE-bench-verified and SWE-bench-live), with careful leakage control (removing issues/commits with overlapping text with test instances).

Thorough ablation studies: episodic-only vs semantic-only vs combined, sensitivity to K in semantic memory construction, and comparison of retrieval methods (BM25 with LLM tokenizer vs standard tokenizer vs dense retrieval), providing useful insights (e.g., sparse retrieval outperforming dense retrieval for code-entity vocabulary).

Goes beyond the localization proxy metric to show downstream impact on end-to-end issue resolution rate using the Agentless patch-generation pipeline, strengthening the practical significance of the results.

Insightful behavioral and efficiency analysis (tool-use shift toward hypothesis-driven investigation, per-example cost variance, correlation between commit-history richness and performance gains) that adds depth beyond aggregate accuracy numbers.
Honest reporting of limitations, including performance degradation in repositories with sparse commit history and acknowledgment of noisy issue-commit linking, which strengthens credibility.
Good reproducibility: detailed tool documentation, example agent trajectories, and prompts provided in appendices.
weaknesses: Evaluation relies on a single, somewhat dated backbone (GPT-4o, 2024-05-13); no experiments demonstrating the approach generalizes across different LLM backbones or model scales, which limits confidence in the generality of the reported gains.

Despite claiming the memory tools are 'modular' and 'easily integrated into existing agentic frameworks,' the paper only demonstrates integration with LocAgent; no actual experiments integrate the memory mechanisms into other frameworks (e.g., Agentless, SWE-agent) to substantiate this generality claim.

The SWE-bench-live evaluation subset is small and pre-filtered (130 examples, instances requiring ≤5 file edits), which may inflate performance and limits how representative the results are of the full, more diverse benchmark.

The technical contribution is somewhat incremental: BM25-based commit retrieval and LLM-generated file summaries are standard techniques: the core novelty lies mainly in the application/framing (repository memory for localization) rather than in new methodology.

No direct comparison against other memory-augmented or experience-driven agent baselines (e.g., the cited SWE-exp) applied to the same localization task, making it hard to contextualize how much of the gain is specific to this design versus general benefit of any memory mechanism.

Semantic memory construction uses a fixed, simplistic 'most frequently edited files' heuristic tuned primarily on a single repository (Django) and then applied uniformly across all repos, despite the paper itself acknowledging more principled JiT-SDP-inspired strategies could improve results.

Performance clearly degrades on repositories with limited commit history (Table 2, 'others' group -13.1), and the paper does not propose or test any mechanism (beyond future-work discussion) to mitigate this failure mode, meaning the method's benefit is conditional and somewhat narrow in scope.
Results appear to be based on single runs without reported variance/statistical significance testing, which is a common concern for agentic benchmark evaluations where trajectories can be stochastic.

strengths: Addresses a well-motivated and under-explored problem: equipping code localization agents with persistent, repository-level memory rather than treating each issue in isolation.

The two-pronged design (episodic memory of commits/issues + semantic memory of file-functionality summaries) is simple, modular, and cleanly integrates into an existing SOTA framework (LocAgent) via additional tool calls, which aids practical adoption.

Experiments span two benchmarks (SWE-bench-verified, SWE-bench-live) with consistent, non-trivial improvements over LocAgent, and include a clean ablation isolating the contribution of each memory component.

Extensive auxiliary analyses are provided: tool-use distribution shifts, per-example/aggregate API cost comparison, sensitivity to the semantic memory size hyperparameter K, retrieval method ablation (sparse vs dense, tokenizer choice), and downstream issue-resolution-rate evaluation using Agentless's patch generation pipeline.
Good situating of the work relative to Just-in-Time Software Defect Prediction and memory-augmented agent literature, drawing a sensible analogy between commit "hotspots" and defect-proneness.
weaknesses: Limited methodological novelty: the core contribution is essentially BM25 retrieval over commit messages/issues plus LLM-generated file summaries bolted onto an existing agent's tool set — a fairly straightforward engineering combination of known techniques (BM25, LLM summarization) rather than a new algorithmic or architectural idea.

Generalizability is questionable: Table 2 shows that for repositories with limited commit history (the "others" group), RepoMem actually hurts performance (-13.1 Acc@5), indicating the method may not transfer well to many real-world repos that lack rich, deep commit histories — a substantial practical limitation that is somewhat downplayed.

Only one backbone LLM (GPT-4o, a dated model as of submission) and only one base agentic framework (LocAgent) are evaluated; no experiments demonstrate the memory mechanism generalizes to other backbones (e.g., open-source or more recent models) or other agentic localization frameworks (OrcaLoca, RepoGraph, etc.), weakening claims of broad applicability.

No comparison or integration with the most directly related prior work on experience/memory-augmented SWE agents (e.g., Chen et al. 2025a, SWE-exp), despite being discussed as the closest related work — an empirical head-to-head is missing, making it hard to assess whether commit-derived memory is actually superior to agent-experience-derived memory.

The downstream issue-resolution-rate gain (37.0% → 40.4%, ~3.4 points) is much more modest than the large Acc@5 localization gains (71.6% → 76.5%), suggesting the practical end-to-end benefit of the proposed memory may be considerably smaller than the headline localization numbers imply.

The coverage analysis in Appendix B.1 (showing high overlap between frequently-edited files and ground-truth buggy files) is somewhat circular/expected given how SWE-bench instances are constructed from historical commits, and this correlation may not hold for genuinely novel bugs or less "hot" codebases, raising concerns about overfitting to a property of the benchmark construction rather than a generalizable insight about defect localization.

Potential data leakage/contamination concerns are only partially addressed; while the authors filter by commit timestamp and textual overlap, GPT-4o's pretraining may already encode knowledge of some of these historical fixes, and this is not discussed or controlled for.

Evaluation metric is restricted to file-level Accuracy@k; no function- or line-level localization results are reported, which is a coarser signal than what is often needed for downstream patch generation.

SWE-bench-live evaluation uses a heavily filtered subset (130 of a larger pool, limited to ≤5 modified files), which may bias the benchmark toward easier/more tractable instances and limits how representative the reported gains are of the full benchmark distribution.

strengths: Addresses a clear and underexplored gap: existing code localization agents are memoryless across repository history, while the paper shows a plausible and intuitive way to leverage commit history as both episodic (past commits/issues) and semantic (hotspot file summaries) memory.

The proposed memory tools (SearchCommit, ExamineCommit, ViewSummary, SearchSummary) are simple, modular, and cleanly integrated into an existing SOTA framework (LocAgent) without requiring retraining.

Experiments span two benchmarks (SWE-bench-verified and SWE-bench-live) and show consistent, non-trivial gains over strong baselines (LocAgent, Agentless, CoRNStack/CodeRankEmbed), with both ablations (episodic-only, semantic-only) supporting the claimed complementarity of the two memory types.

Thorough analysis beyond headline numbers: per-repository breakdown correlating gains with amount of commit history, tool-usage shift analysis, detailed cost/efficiency analysis (including per-instance variance), retrieval method ablation (BM25 vs dense, tokenizer choice), sensitivity to the K hyperparameter, and downstream issue-resolution-rate evaluation via Agentless patch generation pipeline.

Reasonable attention to experimental rigor/reproducibility: explicit commit-history leakage/contamination filtering, documented prompts and tool interfaces in the appendix, and an ethics/reproducibility statement.

Honest discussion of limitations (degraded performance on repos with sparse history, reliance on noisy explicit commit-issue links, fixed-window heuristics) with concrete pointers to future work grounded in the JiT-SDP literature.
weaknesses: Evaluation is limited to a single backbone LLM (GPT-4o, May 2024 snapshot) and a single agentic framework (LocAgent); the generality of the approach to other backbones or other agentic localization frameworks (e.g., OrcaLoca, RepoGraph, SWE-agent-style pipelines) is not empirically demonstrated, which weakens the claim of broad applicability.

Novelty is somewhat incremental: the core techniques (BM25 retrieval over commit messages, LLM-generated file summaries, hotspot identification via commit frequency) are individually well-established (JiT-SDP, RAG, code summarization), and the contribution is primarily the combination/application rather than a fundamentally new method.

No direct empirical comparison against other memory-enhanced agent baselines discussed in related work (e.g., Chen et al. 2025a / SWE-exp, Agent Workflow Memory), despite these being explicitly identified as closely related; this makes it hard to assess whether commit-history-based memory is actually superior to trajectory/experience-based memory for this task.

The hyperparameter K for semantic memory construction is tuned only on a single repository (Django) and then applied uniformly, with no systematic study of how localization gains vary with the richness/size of commit history beyond a coarse post-hoc correlation (Table 2), limiting confidence in generalizability across repos with different scales.

The method clearly degrades for repositories with limited commit history (the 'others' bucket shows a notable drop), and no mitigation or adaptive mechanism (e.g., deciding when to trust/ignore memory) is implemented, only discussed as future work, leaving an important failure mode unresolved.

The end-to-end resolve-rate evaluation (Table 7) is based on only a single Agentless-style pipeline and GPT-4o backbone, so it is unclear how much of the localization improvement actually translates into patch-level gains under more realistic repair pipelines or other LLMs.
